title: Why weren't you Zusya?
hook: Rabbi Zusya fears heaven won't ask why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya (Hasidic tale)

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old man planted a carob tree for grandchildren he'd never meet. Your line was for the ones after. What did you start for someone later? Day fifty-nine.

Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better than you. A better cook. A better parent. Someone your age who's already written the book, run the marathon, started the company. It's easy to feel like you're failing at being them. Two hundred and some years ago, in a small town in Eastern Europe, there lived a Hasidic rabbi named Zusya. He was known for being poor, humble and full of joy. Near the end of his life, his students find him weeping, afraid. They're amazed. What could a man like Zusya possibly fear? Today's story is why weren't you Zusya?
screen: `SOMEONE DOING YOUR LIFE BETTER.` → `RABBI ZUSYA, WEEPING.` → `WHAT COULD HE FEAR?`

segments.voice: Rabbi, the students say, why are you afraid? You've been as faithful as Moses. As kind as Abraham. And Zusya answers: when I come before the heavenly court, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? I'd have an answer for that: I wasn't given what Moses was given. They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham? I wasn't Abraham. They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say then? That's the whole story. It comes from the Hasidic movement, the joyful, mystical renewal that spread through Jewish communities in Eastern Europe in the seventeen and eighteen hundreds. Its stories were told aloud for generations before they were written down, and Zusya of Hanipol, who died around 1800, is one of its best-loved figures. The tale is known around the world today largely through collections like Martin Buber's. Here's why it lands so hard. We usually measure ourselves against someone else, the greatest person we can imagine, and we always come up short. Zusya says that isn't the test. Nobody will ask you to be Moses. The question is harder and kinder at the same time: did you become the person only you could be? Did you use what you were actually given? Your hands, your voice, your odd mix of gifts and wounds? It's harder, because you can't hide behind I'm not Moses. It's kinder, because nobody is asking you to be anyone else. There's exactly one Zusya. And exactly one you.
screen: `WHY WEREN'T YOU MOSES?` · `A TALE FROM THE HASIDIM.` · `WE MEASURE AGAINST SOMEONE ELSE.` · `HARDER, AND KINDER.` · then, large: `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing only you would do. For now, settle, and breathe. Let go of the person you've been comparing yourself to. Let them walk off. Then ask quietly: what do I have that's mine? A way of making people laugh. A particular kindness. Something you notice that others don't. Pick one, and think of one small way to use it today, the way only you would. The bell holds the time.
Why weren't you Zusya? The question Rabbi Zusya feared: not why weren't you someone greater, but why weren't you yourself. Today's word.
Your line: be zusya. Today, when you catch yourself wishing you were someone else, stop, and do one thing the way only you would do it. Day fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Zusya's question is one of the most quoted Hasidic sayings, told in synagogues, sermons and graduation speeches, and Hasidic tales like it are still passed on aloud in Hasidic communities.
